text: Alberto Di Maria is a freelance engineer who works remotely, on US hours. He builds AI products end-to-end, in three areas: voice agents, AI automations, and sites and platforms. Voice agents (AI phone assistants that hold a whole conversation) are his specialty within that offer.

His background bridges audio and machine learning. He holds a Master's degree (thesis on benchmarking generative music models) and has worked on audio software and signal processing, including a period as an Audio Developer at Anecoica Studio and a workshop with the Music Technology Group (MTG) in Barcelona.

Core strengths: real-time voice pipelines (barge-in, low latency, turn-taking), agentic tool-calling, retrieval-augmented generation, full-stack web (Next.js, Supabase, Stripe), and the engineering rigor that proves a system works — evaluation suites, latency metrics (p50/p95), tests, CI and observability.

He is the kind of engineer who measures what he builds: not "it seems to work" but eval scores, success rates and latency percentiles. He cares about cost-consciousness, security hygiene, and shipping things that are genuinely production-ready.
Contact: ing.albertodimaria@gmail.com. Portfolio: albertodimaria.com.

Beat Store is a producer's online store, built by Alberto for a paying client: producers sell beats with tiered licenses. It was designed with Laura Zanchetta, a UI/UX designer, and built from her Figma file. It is a large project and the full-stack counterpart to his AI work. The store is delivered and visible as a preview; it launches on the producer's own domain in early 2027.

Stack: Next.js, TypeScript, Supabase, Stripe for payments, deployed on Netlify, with PostHog analytics and Google login. Features include a cart with bundle promotions (buy 3 / 5 / 8), license tiers, an admin dashboard, and producer management.

The standout is the hardening pass for production rigor. Starting from a codebase with no tests and no CI, Alberto added: 34 money-path tests (Vitest unit tests plus Playwright end-to-end), reaching about 86% statement coverage and 100% function coverage on the money path — checkout, Stripe webhook signature and idempotency, bundle pricing, license PDF contracts. He added a GitHub Actions CI pipeline (typecheck, lint, test, e2e) that gates every push, and Sentry for error tracking and p95 latency.

Security was already solid before hardening: Stripe webhook signature verification and idempotency, server-side pricing (never trusting client amounts). The hardening was about proving correctness with tests and measuring it with observability — turning "ships on vibes" into "ships with evidence".
Company Brain is a tool-calling business agent Alberto built at an Italian hackathon, where it placed in the Top 10 of 80+ builders, qualifying for the national Hackathon League.

The idea: a single agent that acts as the "brain" of a company, answering questions and taking actions across the business by calling tools (querying data, running operations) rather than just chatting. It showcases agentic tool-calling applied to a real business context — the agent decides which tool to invoke to satisfy a request, chains calls, and returns grounded answers.

It sits in the same family as Alberto's other agentic work (Shy Order's multi-agent orchestration, Dance Voice Agent's parallel tool-calling): the throughline is an LLM that doesn't just talk but acts, with the orchestration logic and tool contracts engineered deliberately rather than left to chance.

Dance Voice Agent is Alberto's flagship voice project: a phone agent he built for a dance school. It recognises the caller, books classes, cancels and reschedules, and hands over to a person when it should. It is a finished build, tested with automated calls; it is not taking the school's calls yet. The site shows one recorded test call, with its transcript and timings, right under the hero.

Architecture: the agent runs natively on the ElevenLabs Agents platform (ConvAI), with Qwen 3.5 397B as the brain and Eleven v3 Conversational as the voice, in Italian and Spanish. Its thirteen tools are Postgres functions called straight over PostgREST, so the business logic lives in the database and there is no application server in the hot path. A conversation-initiation webhook (a Deno edge function) resolves the caller's number to a student before the call is even answered, which is why the agent can greet people by name instead of asking who they are halfway through. The platform guarantees turn-taking, barge-in and latency.
Stack: ElevenLabs Agents, Qwen 3.5 397B, Supabase (Postgres, with the agent's tools as RPC functions), Deno edge functions, Twilio for telephony, a Next.js admin dashboard on Vercel.

What makes it a flagship is how it is tested. Alberto treats the agent like a model, not like a website: an adversarial suite of scenarios runs against the live agent and every scenario is repeated, because on an LLM a single green run is an anecdote rather than a result. Each change is gated by a score. What the platform can guarantee is never asked of the prompt: caller recognition and the trial-week flag are verified by deterministic checks outside the model, and the tools return a count plus one course instead of a list, so the agent physically cannot read twelve courses down the phone. The agent answers about 0.9 seconds after the caller stops speaking. Per-turn latency and cost are instrumented and persisted, and an admin dashboard shows call analytics, booking trends and containment.

The prompt lives in git, not only on the platform: it is pulled, diffed and pushed by a sync script, so a change can be reviewed and rolled back like any other code. The repository is public (anonymized) and includes a STUDY_GUIDE documenting the architecture, the latency budget and the design decisions.

Lyra is a lyrics-first music discovery experience, built at the Musixmatch hackathon (the "Musicathon") with a teammate. Instead of recommending tracks by audio features alone, Lyra centers the lyrics: it surfaces music through what the words say and the emotion they carry, and for each track it cites one specific lyric line that matches.

The interface is a wheel of emotions with curved, clickable labels rendered as SVG textPaths along arcs. Under it sits an emotion-buffer model: a FIFO of the last few moods, weighted so a repeated mood counts double, with a positional weighting that gives the first pick the strongest pull. The playlist starts once a few moods are selected and updates as the user spins the wheel.

Stack: Next.js 16, TypeScript, react-three-fiber for the 3D/interactive layer, with an Anthropic Claude agent on the backend and a Musixmatch recommendation backend, deployed on Vercel with the backend on Hugging Face Spaces.
Lyra is Alberto's most creative, design-forward project — where audio, ML and a crafted interactive front end meet. It's also where he first worked seriously with react-three-fiber.

Shy Order is a multi-agent system that calls restaurants on the user's behalf to book a table — for people who would rather not make the phone call themselves. The user states what they want; the agent finds the restaurant, places the call, talks to the staff, and reports back.

It runs on ElevenLabs Conversational AI for the voice side. Restaurant discovery uses LLM-based extraction: instead of brittle regex/HTML scraping, an LLM with a forced tool call pulls the phone number and details from the restaurant's web presence. A concrete bug Alberto found and fixed: phone numbers that lived only inside a `tel:` link (not in visible text) were being missed, so he passed the `tel:` hrefs to the LLM as hints.
Stack: Python, FastAPI, Twilio, Supabase, with an admin dashboard. The system separates the conversation into implicit phases (talking to the user vs talking to the restaurant).

Shy Order demonstrates multi-agent orchestration and robust real-world tool use — the messy reality of getting structured data (a working phone number) out of unstructured web pages, and driving a real phone conversation to a goal.

Alberto's Master's thesis (Metatron) is an empirical, hands-on benchmark of generative music models. Rather than reporting benchmark numbers from papers, he evaluated a range of generative models himself — exploring text-to-music and audio generation systems such as MusicGen, Stable Audio, RAVE and MusicVAE, and using audio embeddings (Essentia, TensorFlow) for analysis.

He evaluated around thirteen generative models hands-on, under real hardware constraints (ROCm/CUDA), documenting what each could and couldn't do in practice — including how hard certain explorations (like VAE latent spaces) turned out to be. The framing is empirical evaluation from direct use, not benchmark-table citation.

The thesis sits under Education with a research slant, and it is single-authored: Alberto did the work from scratch. It connects his audio background to the generative-AI wave, and it's the project that most directly shows research-style rigor — designing an evaluation, running it, and reporting honest findings about model capabilities and limits.

Alberto offers three services. 1) Voice agents: phone agents that answer and call out, or voice inside an app. 2) AI automations: automations that close repetitive work, and agents that answer questions on a company's own data with exact numbers. 3) Sites and platforms: a new site from scratch, or an existing one updated and fixed.

Each service is shown next to its two best pieces of work. Voice agents: the phone agent for a dance school and Shy Order (also Collaudio and Parlando). AI automations: Company Brain and Zero to HubSpot (also Beat Agent and Invoice Agent). Sites and platforms: Beat Store and Alex Bartok Music (also filoconduttore). Visitors can open each block in the work section.

Working with Alberto follows four steps: 1) a free intro call to understand the problem; 2) a clear proposal with a fixed price agreed upfront — no surprises, no hourly billing; 3) the build, with demos and updates along the way; 4) delivery, with training on how to use it and support after release. Pricing is discussed in the call, not published on the site.

To start a project: book a call from the site (the first call is free), use the contact form (name, email, message) or email ing.albertodimaria@gmail.com. Alberto usually replies within a day. The visitor can also ask D10S (this assistant) to draft the contact message for them: D10S can pre-fill the form with a summary of their need, and the visitor reviews and sends it themselves.

Right under the hero the site shows one recorded test call to the dance-school phone agent, 87 seconds long, with the full transcript, the time of every reply and the tools the agent called. The caller asks for a beginner class on the Thursday in two weeks, not this Thursday; the agent looks up the courses, proposes three, and books Bachata and Salsa on Thursday 19 November at 19:00. The agent answers in about 0.9 seconds and the booking is written at 1:05. The visitor can play it at normal or double speed, and D10S can play it for them.
Alberto builds voice agents for agencies. Every agent is tested by automated calls and then verified by hand before delivery.

Collaudio is an automated tester for voice agents, built by Alberto. It phones the agent itself, holds the conversation, and checks what the agent said against what actually happened in the database. It was born while working with a client who builds outbound agents, where every change meant making calls by hand. It runs in-house, with no third-party provider. In its test runs it caught 9 bugs out of 10 with no false alarms.

Parlando is a voice-first language tutor for English and Spanish, built solo by Alberto: Android app, backend and admin dashboard. You talk to it; it listens, corrects and remembers each learner's mistakes, and picks the next scenario with spaced repetition. It is in private beta.

filoconduttore (filoconduttore.it) is Alberto's tutoring material turned into a study site: more than 130 lessons in electronics and computer science, with a voice agent that gives oral tests. It comes from his work as a private tutor of university students.

Zero to HubSpot is a HubSpot-compatible CRM Alberto built in five hours at the national final of the Italian Hackathon League, where it placed in the Top 25. It migrated 15 years of data from a legacy CRM in 35 seconds. He qualified for the final with Company Brain.
Alex Bartok Music (alexbartokmusic.com) is client work: a musician's broken website rebuilt from scratch, in three languages, with a paid client area.
